Return
rē-tûrn´
v. (to come back to a place, state, or person; rendering Hebrew shuwb, Greek hupostrepho)
From French retourner, to turn again. Scripture bends the word two ways at once: man returns to the dust by the curse, and man returns to the LORD by mercy — and the second is the only escape from the first.

Biblical Definition

Return is turn with a homeward direction: the going back to a place one came from, or a Person one has left. The curse gave the word its first and heaviest sense: “till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return” (Genesis 3:19). Every man is already on a return journey, and left to himself it ends in the dust he was taken from. Against that the prophets set the other return, and they set it with a promise of abundance: “Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon” (Isaiah 55:7). Two things must go before the returning — a forsaken way and forsaken thoughts — and two things follow it, mercy and abundant pardon. The LORD calls even the unfaithful back by name: “Return, thou backsliding Israel, saith the LORD; and I will not cause mine anger to fall upon you: for I am merciful” (Jeremiah 3:12). The soul's own returning is addressed to itself in the Psalms: “Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for the LORD hath dealt bountifully with thee” (Psalm 116:7), where rest is a place the soul has wandered from and may come home to.

Webster 1828 Definition

To come or go back to the same place or state; to revert; to repay or render back. In Scripture the word carries both the curse's return to dust and the sinner's return to the LORD, who abundantly pardons.

expand to see more

RETURN, v.i. [Fr. retourner; re and tourner, to turn.] To come or go back to the same place from which one departed; as, to return from a journey.

2. To come back to the same state or condition; as, to return to a former practice.

3. To answer; to reply; to make a reply or report.

RETURN, v.t. To bring, carry or send back; as, to return a borrowed book.

2. To repay; to give in requital or recompense; as, to return good for evil.

3. To render back or transmit officially; as, to return a writ; to return an account.

Key Scripture

Genesis 3:19 — "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return."

Isaiah 55:7 — "Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon."

Jeremiah 3:12 — "Go and proclaim these words toward the north, and say, Return, thou backsliding Israel, saith the LORD; and I will not cause mine anger to fall upon you: for I am merciful, saith the LORD, and I will not keep anger for ever."

Psalm 116:7 — "Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for the LORD hath dealt bountifully with thee."

Modern Corruption

Return has been sentimentalized into homecoming without repentance — a warm reunion that skips the forsaken way and the forsaken thoughts Isaiah puts before it.

expand to see more

Much modern preaching on returning to God keeps the affection and drops the terms. The prodigal is invoked, the Father's run and kiss are dwelt upon, and the son's own confession is passed over. Isaiah 55:7 does not permit it: the wicked forsakes his way and the unrighteous man his thoughts, and then returns. Mercy and abundant pardon are promised on the far side of that forsaking, not instead of it. Where the terms are dropped, hearers are taught to expect the welcome without the turning, and the doctrine of repentance quietly disappears while its warmest illustration is retold.

There is a second and colder error that treats Genesis 3:19 as the whole story — man returns to dust, and nothing further is to be said. That is the creed of the age in its plainest form, and it is why the modern funeral so often has nothing to say. Scripture holds both returns together and subordinates the first to the second: the body goes to the ground under the curse, and the soul is called home to its rest because “the LORD hath dealt bountifully” (Psalm 116:7). Recover the pairing, and the word regains its weight in both directions.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shuwb (to turn back, return) serves both the curse's return to dust and the covenant call to return to the LORD; Greek hupostrepho (to turn back) and anastrepho (to turn again) carry the ordinary sense in the New Testament.

expand to see more

Hebrew shuwb (H7725) — to turn back, return, restore; the single verb behind Isaiah's call and Jeremiah's summons to backsliding Israel.

Hebrew meshuwbah (H4878) — backsliding, turning away; the noun formed from shuwb, naming the condition the return reverses.

Hebrew 'adamah (H127) — ground, earth; the destination of the curse's return in Genesis 3:19.

Greek hupostrepho (G5290) — to turn back, to return; the narrative verb of the Gospels and Acts.

Greek epistrophe (G1995) — a turning about, conversion; the noun naming the return as an accomplished thing.

Usage

"“Unto dust shalt thou return” — the curse states a return no man escapes by his own strength."

"“Let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him” — the terms precede the promise."

"“Return unto thy rest, O my soul” — the believer preaches the word to his own soul."
